**Self** — what a self is — the minimal, bodily and pre-reflective self, self-models and the sense of being a subject, the self as process or as context, and whether machines or groups can be selves. Not the person, which is personhood (group: philosophy; ADR-024).

| [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md) v4 | The Extended Mind | Clark & Chalmers (1998), DOI-10.1093/analys/58.1.7. The paper argues from a functionalist parity claim that a process or standing state which would count as cognitive if it happened in the head counts as cognitive when an external resource carries it, provided the resource is actively coupled to the organism here and now. Otto's notebook entry is its example of such a standing belief. From this it infers, in one paragraph, that the self extends too. The four "criteria" for a coupled resource (constancy, direct availability, automatic endorsement, and the admittedly "arguable" past conscious endorsement) are offered as the features that make the paradigm case clear. The paper explicitly says they are not necessary and sufficient conditions. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-180](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-180.md)); it is worth reading as the source text of the extended-mind thesis, and it is short. Its constitutive conclusion follows from a role-functionalism about belief and a parity principle that the paper states rather than defends, so a reader should take it as the origin of the debate and not as its settlement. |
| [LIT-136](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-136.md) v2 | The Informational Nature of Personal Identity | Floridi (2011), DOI-10.1007/s11023-011-9259-6. Floridi deflates the diachronic question of personal identity, holding that sameness is always relative to a purpose-fixed level of abstraction and that metaphysical versions of the question "do not deserve to be taken seriously" (p. 554). He puts the synchronic question first: what binds a self's information into a unity. His answer is an admittedly "figurative" 3C model in which the self is the last of three successive encapsulations, corporeal (bonded by chemical bonds), cognitive (bonded by mutual information) and conscious (bonded by semantics, and so dependent on a community). He then reads ICTs as "egopoietic" technologies because they act on all three membranes. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-130](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-130.md)); worth reading as the programmatic statement of Floridi's informational, level-of-abstraction approach to the self and its link to his information ethics; its central model is a self-described figure, not an argued theory, and the individuation-first thesis is asserted in a few lines. |
| [LIT-292](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-292.md) v2 | Identification and Identity | Velleman (2002), DOI-10.7551/mitpress/2143.003.0007. Velleman targets Frankfurt's *later* conception of autonomy. On that conception, a person acts autonomously only when his volitions derive from "the essential character of his will", and that essence consists of volitional necessities that are also the conditions of his personal identity. Velleman argues against it on three grounds. Such an essence would ground authenticity, not autonomy (the Winnicottian False Self is inauthentic but over-controlled). Frankfurt offers no argument or example that motivational change ends a person. And the ideal of wholeheartedness, which cures ambivalence by extruding a desire from the self, is a defensive fantasy: Freud's Rat Man was made ill by just such a separation, and identifying with part of oneself in the ordinary, imaginative sense is Sartrean bad faith. He replaces "the self" with an *aspectual* reading of "self" as a marker of reflexivity. On that reading autonomy is behaviour motivated partly by the understanding, the part of us "with which we cannot help identifying", without its being our identity (pp. 357–360). | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 ([NOTE-268](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-268.md)); worth reading as the sharpest critique of Frankfurt's late (1990s) identification of autonomy with a volitional essence, and as a careful source for what Frankfurt said in the essays collected in *Necessity, Volition, and Love* (1999). It is not a survey of the 1971–1987 hierarchical account, which it summarizes in one paragraph and defers to "What Happens When Someone Acts?"; its positive view is stated "briefly" and explicitly deferred to other essays. |

| [LIT-405](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-405.md) | Where Am I? | Dennett (1978), the closing essay of Brainstorms. A narrator's brain ("Yorick") is kept in a vat in Houston and radio-linked to his body ("Hamlet") under Tulsa. Where is he? Not simply where the body is, and not simply where the brain is: he cannot think "here" of the vat. He favours being wherever his point of view is, finds that unclear, and when the links fail finds himself "in Houston". A computer duplicate ("Hubert") runs in step with Yorick, and either can drive a new body with no detectable switch. The essay ends when the two drift out of step and a second person speaks through the body. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-338](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-338.md)), in a retyped course copy, not the printed book; worth reading as the founding thought experiment on where a person is when brain and body are apart, and the place the record's threads on extended vehicles, scattered individuals and functional duplicates meet. It is fiction with a philosophical argument inside it. It tries three answers to "where am I?" (where the body is, where the brain is, where the point of view is), favours the third, admits it is unclear, and ends by showing that two synchronised brains can drift into two persons. It argues by intuition pump and settles nothing; the narrator calls one of its answers a truth "of underwhelming significance". |

| [LIT-432](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-432.md) | The Emotion Machine: Commonsense Thinking, Artificial Intelligence, and the Future of the Human Mind | Minsky (2006), Simon & Schuster, read in the author's 2005 draft. Emotions are Ways to Think, not a separate faculty. Each emotional state turns some mental resources on and others off, by Selectors that Critics trigger when they recognise a type of problem. The same machinery serves ordinary thinking. The book adds six levels of mental activity, from instinctive reaction to self-conscious reflection. It treats "consciousness", "emotion" and "pain" as suitcase words for many processes, and the Self as a network of partial self-models. It is a design argued from examples. Against Damasio, it treats the body as one more resource the brain uses, not the stuff of emotion. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 in the author's posted draft of 2005 ([NOTE-348](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-348.md)), not in the published book; worth reading as the late, fullest statement of the Society of Mind programme. It is the one where emotion is put inside thinking: an emotional state is a selection of mental resources switched on and off, made by Selectors that Critics trigger, and so it is a Way to Think. Read it as a design proposal argued by examples, not as evidence. It reports no experiment, Minsky labels several of its central ideas his own conjectures, and it sets the body to the side of emotion, against the bodily account of Damasio ([LIT-384](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-384.md), [LIT-388](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-388.md)) that this record holds. |

| [LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md) | Self models | Metzinger (2007, rev. 2013), Scholarpedia 2(10):4174. There is no substantial self, only a phenomenal self-model (PSM): the conscious part of an organism's self-model, an instrument of global control. A phenomenal self arises "if and only if a system operates under a transparent PSM", one it cannot introspectively recognise as a model; a first-person perspective is a transparent model of the intentionality relation (PMIR). Self-models can be unconscious and artificial, as in Bongard, Zykov and Lipson's limping starfish robot; embodiment comes in three orders, the third conscious. | [LIT-451](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-451.md) | Of Personal Identity | Hume (1739), Treatise 1.4.6, with the Appendix (1740). There is no impression of a self, "constant and invariable", so no idea of one: introspection finds only "some particular perception or other", and the mind is "a bundle or collection of different perceptions". The identity we ascribe to it is "fictitious", like that of plants, ships and churches: an easy transition of the imagination along resemblance and causation, with memory discovering rather than producing it, so that hard cases are "grammatical" rather than philosophical. The Appendix retracts the account of the connecting principle: two principles he cannot reconcile or renounce leave the matter "too hard for my understanding". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-386](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-386.md)), in the Merivale–Millican critical text on davidhume.org, with the Appendix's second thoughts (App. 10–21); worth reading as the founding statement of the bundle view and the first published retraction of it. The section finds no impression of a self, calls the mind "a bundle or collection of different perceptions", and explains our ascription of identity to it as a fiction of the imagination run on resemblance and causation, the same fiction that makes a repaired ship or a rebuilt church "the same". The Appendix then confesses that it cannot explain what unites the perceptions and leaves the problem "too hard for my understanding". The section's case is introspective and associationist; its Appendix is the clearest statement of what any bundle view owes. |
| [LIT-452](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-452.md) | Against Narrativity | Strawson (2004), Ratio 17(4):428–452. Rejects both the psychological Narrativity thesis (people do experience their lives as a story) and the ethical one (they should, to be full persons), naming Sacks, Bruner, Dennett, Taylor, MacIntyre and Schechtman. Distinguishes Diachronic self-experience (the self I am now was there in the past) from Episodic (it was not, though the human being was), and splits Narrativity into form-finding, story-telling and revision, with only story-telling sufficient. Episodics are normal and can live well; self-narration risks falsifying the self it describes. Argued from the author's own case. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-383](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-383.md)), in the published typeset text; worth reading as the standard objection to narrative accounts of the self, and for its distinctions: Episodic versus Diachronic self-experience, and form-finding, story-telling and revision as separable parts of "Narrativity". Read it as a report of a temperament argued from the author's own case and literary examples. Its empirical claims (a genetic "individual difference variable", the spread across cultures) are asserted, not shown, and its central metaphysical claim, that the remoter past did not happen to "me*", is stated rather than argued. |
| [LIT-453](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-453.md) | Philosophical conceptions of the self: implications for cognitive science | Gallagher (2000), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 4(1):14–21. Divides philosophical accounts of the self into the "minimal self", accessible to present self-consciousness without temporal extension, and the "narrative self", extended in time through memory and story. The minimal self splits into a sense of ownership and a sense of agency, which come apart in involuntary movement and, after Frith, in schizophrenic thought insertion when a forward comparator fails. Neonatal imitation suggests an embodied minimal self; Strawson's and Tani's are momentary. Against Dennett's narrative centre, the self is "the sum total of its narratives". Read in the author's preprint. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-377](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-377.md)), in the author's preprint, not the typeset article; worth reading as the paper that set the minimal self against the narrative self for cognitive science, and for the split of the minimal self into a sense of ownership and a sense of agency, which it ties to Frith's comparator model of schizophrenic thought insertion. Per its publisher, a theory of social categories built on the question "what is it for a feature of an individual to be socially meaningful?"; its main idea is that "social categories are conferred upon people", and its "conferralist" framework is applied to sex, gender, race, disability and other categories, and to their tendency to oppress. Unread: filed from the description and contents only. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is not open access, Oxford Academic is paywalled, and the author's site posts replies and related essays but no chapters or drafts), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. | [LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md) | Relational Frame Theory: Some Implications for Understanding and Treating Human Psychopathology | Barnes-Holmes, Barnes-Holmes, McHugh & Hayes (2004), International Journal of Psychology and Psychological Therapy 4(2):355–375. RFT stated briefly: humans relate events bidirectionally and arbitrarily, as a generalized operant under contextual control, so words take on the functions of what they are related to. Frames combine into networks, networks are related to networks (metaphor), rules are networks that regulate behaviour, and the self is content, process and context of verbal relations. Psychopathology is read as verbal behaviour, and ACT's acceptance, defusion and values are given RFT interpretations. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-430](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-430.md)), in place of the RFT book, [LIT-549](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-549.md); worth reading as a short statement of Relational Frame Theory by two of the book's editors, and as the paper that shows how RFT is meant to become a theory of psychopathology. Humans, unlike the animals of conditioning research, relate events bidirectionally, so a word acquires the functions of what it names. Relating is a generalized operant learned across exemplars, and its frames share mutual entailment, combinatorial entailment and the transformation of function. Rules are relational networks, and the self is three verbal relations to one's own behaviour. ACT's acceptance, defusion and values are then reinterpreted in those terms. Its clinical examples are illustrations, not data, and it says its Part 3 is "no more than a heuristic". |

The founding book of Relational Frame Theory: human language and cognition are learned, generalized operant behaviour, the arbitrarily applicable relating of events (mutually, in combination, and with transformation of their functions) under contextual control. Eight chapters state the theory, from derived relations to rules and the self; five apply it to development, education, social processes, psychopathology and religion. The ACT model: psychopathology is psychological inflexibility, produced when language (cognitive fusion) and experiential avoidance dominate direct contingencies, and ACT restores flexibility through six processes. A review of correlational, component, mediational and outcome studies finds the model "broadly supportive" but the literature immature, and the evidence suggests ACT works through different processes from traditional CBT. Read in an early author manuscript whose numbers differ from the published paper's. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-431](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-431.md)), but in an early manuscript, not the published text; worth reading as the canonical statement of the ACT model of psychopathology, "psychological inflexibility", and of the six processes ACT targets. Cognitive fusion and experiential avoidance (from [LIT-551](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-551.md)) narrow behaviour, and acceptance, defusion, present-moment contact, self as context, values and committed action restore flexibility. The copy read is an author manuscript in Georgia State University's repository that still carries "xx" placeholders, and its numbers differ from the published paper's as Kashdan and Rottenberg report them (21 studies against 32; an AAQ correlation printed ".030" against ".42"). | [LIT-558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-558.md) | The "What" and "Why" of Goal Pursuits: Human Needs and the Self-Determination of Behavior | Deci & Ryan (2000), Psychological Inquiry 11(4):227–268, target article. SDT's case for innate psychological needs, for competence, relatedness and autonomy, defined as nutriments for growth, integrity and well-being and identified functionally, against Hull's drives and Murray's acquired needs. The "why" of a goal (autonomous or controlled regulation) and its "what" (intrinsic or extrinsic aspiration) each predict well-being, because each affects need satisfaction. Thwarted needs yield substitutes, controlled styles and rigid patterns. SDT grounds autonomy in the organism's tendency to self-organize, argued to be an evolved advantage. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-439](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-439.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the published target article on selfdeterminationtheory.org; worth reading as the full statement of what SDT means by a "need" and why it posits three. Needs are "innate psychological nutriments that are essential for ongoing psychological growth, integrity, and well-being" (p. 228), identified by what follows when they are satisfied or thwarted, not by how strongly people want them. Goals differ in their "why" (autonomous or controlled regulation) and their "what" (intrinsic or extrinsic content), and both matter because of need satisfaction. Thwarting produces need substitutes, controlled regulatory styles and rigid behaviour patterns. It is a target article: the commentaries and the authors' reply in the same issue were not read. |

Self-determination theory in eleven pages. Three innate psychological needs, for competence, autonomy and relatedness, must be satisfied for growth, integration and well-being; their thwarting is "a principal source of human distress" (p. 74). Motivation differs in kind, not only amount: extrinsic motivation runs from external through introjected and identified to integrated regulation, and becomes more autonomous as a regulation is internalized and integrated with the self. Autonomy is volition, not independence. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-442](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-442.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the published article on selfdeterminationtheory.org; worth reading as the shortest statement of self-determination theory by its authors, and the one most cited. It gives the three basic psychological needs (competence, autonomy, relatedness), the continuum of regulation from amotivation through external, introjected, identified and integrated regulation to intrinsic motivation, and the claim that autonomy is volition, "not ... being independent, detached, or selfish" (p. 74). It is a review: every empirical claim is cited to other papers, nothing is tested here, and it states the reward-undermining result as settled by Deci, Koestner & Ryan ([LIT-557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-557.md)), which Cameron, Banko & Pierce dispute ([LIT-562](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-562.md), unread; by its abstract). |
| [LIT-560](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-560.md) | Self-Regulation and the Problem of Human Autonomy: Does Psychology Need Choice, Self-Determination, and Will? | Ryan & Deci (2006), Journal of Personality 74(6):1557–1586. SDT's defence of autonomy as a psychological construct. Philosophers (phenomenologists from Pfänder and Ricoeur; hierarchical accounts from Frankfurt and Dworkin) agree that autonomy is self-endorsement, not independence. On that definition, the critiques fail: behaviourists and Bandura define autonomy as independence from the environment; reductive neuroscience mistakes levels of explanation; nonconscious priming shows autonomy can be compromised, not that it is illusory; too many options is not self-determination; and autonomy matters across cultures. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-441](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-441.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the published article on selfdeterminationtheory.org; worth reading as the place where SDT states its concept of autonomy against both philosophy and psychology. Autonomy is "regulation by the self", its opposite "heteronomy", regulation "without self-endorsement" (abstract). It is "a matter of degree" (p. 1562), compatible with dependence and with having one option, and lies "not in being independent causes but in exercising their capacity to reflectively endorse or reject prompted actions" (p. 1573). It answers Skinner, Bandura, Pinker, Bargh, Wegner, Schwartz and Iyengar. Its engagement with Frankfurt is thin: two citations of the 1971 paper inside one paragraph on hierarchical accounts, with the analytic detail taken from Dworkin. |
| [LIT-568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-568.md) | Précis: Being No One | Metzinger (2005), PSYCHE 11(5), the author's précis of Being No One. Minimal consciousness is a global world-model in a window of presence that cannot be recognised as a model (globality, presentationality, transparency). A phenomenal self is a transparent self-model: "no such things as selves exist in the world". Transparency comes in degrees, and the self-model's opaque partition is what lets humans doubt their own self-representation. The unity of consciousness is a single global functional cluster. A first-person perspective is a phenomenal model of the intentionality relation, and iterating it yields introspective and social intelligence. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-460](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-460.md)), as the read substitute for Being No One ([LIT-467](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-467.md)), which it summarises in Metzinger's own words. Phenomenal selfhood is a transparent self-model, "a function realized by a lack of information"; "no such things as selves exist in the world". The unity of a conscious world is a global functional cluster bound by "highest-order binding". IFS views a person as "an ecology of relatively discrete minds", each wanting a valuable role but forced into extreme ones by experience: managers keep control, exiles carry pain, and firefighters douse exiles' feelings by bingeing or numbing. | [LIT-586](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-586.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Ainslie (2005), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28(5), the précis of Breakdown of Will (2001). People and other animals discount delayed rewards hyperbolically, so preferences reverse as a smaller, sooner reward comes near, and a person becomes a population of reward-seeking "interests" that must forestall one another. Willpower is the bundling of future choices by treating the present one as a precedent: an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma, not an organ or a top-down ego. The same recursion predicts the will's costs: legalism, circumscribed "lapse districts", motivated blindness to lapses, and rules that favour countable goals over subtle ones. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md)), as the substitute for the 2001 book ([LIT-583](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-583.md)), which the owner suggested and which the précis follows chapter by chapter. Worth reading as the shortest complete statement of picoeconomics in Ainslie's own words. Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse as a smaller, sooner reward draws near, so a person behaves like a population of "interests" that bargain across time. Will is not a faculty above them but a recursive self-prediction: treating each choice as a precedent "bundles" future rewards, an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma in which "credibility is power". The same mechanism predicts the will's side effects: legalism, "lapse districts", motivated misperception and compulsive over-control. |

| [LIT-626](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-626.md) | Three types of phenomenal consciousness and their functional roles: unfolding the ALARM theory of consciousness | Newen & Montemayor (2025), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 380:20240314. The ALARM theory: phenomenal consciousness has two levels of experience and three functions. Basic arousal, realisable without cortex, alarms the body when a homeostatic variable leaves its tolerance range, overriding slow regulation with no choice involved; it adds lasting care for the injury and one-shot, generalised avoidance learning. General alertness, cortical and attention-guided, enables flexible learning and decision-making. Reflexive self-consciousness is general alertness with metacognitive self-relational content, not a third kind of experience, and enables long-term planning that accounts for one's own and others' mindsets. IIT, higher-order theories and GNWT are faulted for tying consciousness to neocortex and leaving basic arousal out. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-489](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-489.md)); worth reading as the shortest statement of the ALARM theory: phenomenal consciousness has two levels of experience, basic arousal (subcortical, an alarm that overrides slow homeostatic regulation) and general alertness (cortical, attention-guided, for flexible learning and choice), plus reflexive self-consciousness, which is general alertness with metacognitive self-relational content and its own function, long-term planning. Its evidence is a short list of cited findings (hydranencephaly, decorticate cats, central lateral thalamus stimulation in macaques), and the functional claims are argued, not tested. |
| [LIT-628](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-628.md) | Homeostatic feelings and the biology of consciousness | Damasio & Damasio (2022), Brain 145(7):2231–2235, an Essay. Consciousness occurs when mind contents are spontaneously identified as belonging to their organism, and a continuous flow of homeostatic feelings (hunger, pain, well-being, plain feelings of existence) supplies that identification and "lends" consciousness to exteroceptive images. Feelings are hybrid: interoceptive pathways are unmyelinated, partly non-synaptic and unprotected by a blood–brain barrier, so the body and its neural map interact directly. Posterior brainstem lesions abolish consciousness where large cortical ones may not; consciousness needs "a partnership of nervous systems with the bodies they serve". | Active — skimmed 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-507](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-507.md)): every section was covered, but through a fetch tool that returned section-by-section accounts with short quotes, not a verbatim copy, so the quotes are unchecked; worth reading as the shortest complete statement of the Damasios' claim that consciousness is the spontaneous identification of mind contents as one's own, supplied by a continuous flow of homeostatic feelings, which are hybrid: in interoception the map and the body it maps interact and "commingle". It is a five-page Essay with no data. Its evidence is clinical and cited (brainstem coma versus cortical lesions, general anaesthesia), and its mechanism is the cellular contrast in Table 1: unmyelinated, non-synaptic, barrier-free interoceptive pathways. |
| [LIT-650](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-650.md) | Conscious birds | Maldarelli & Güntürkün (2025), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 380:20240308. A review arguing that birds show sensory awareness (bistable perception in pigeons; crow nidopallium caudolaterale neurons that follow the reported percept, not the stimulus) and graded self-awareness (magpie and house crow mark tests; pigeons and roosters that treat their mirror image as not-a-conspecific while failing the mark test). Checked against three theories, the avian brain meets the anatomical and physiological requirements of the global neuronal workspace (a hub-and-module connectome with NCL as hub) and of recurrent processing, while IIT's have not been tested (no PCI, no grid-like lattice found). The authors say the evidence does not yet allow a strong conclusion. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-488](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-488.md)); worth reading as a short, current statement of the case for consciousness in birds and of what each of three theories (global neuronal workspace, recurrent processing, IIT) would need to find in an avian brain. Its strongest evidence is second-hand: crow nidopallium caudolaterale neurons that track the reported percept rather than the stimulus (Nieder et al. 2020). Its sharpest argument is that the bird's prefrontal analogue is nuclear, not laminar, so conscious report does not need cortical layering. The authors say the findings "do not allow for a strong conclusion". |

The chapter is paywalled at Oxford Academic, Unpaywall finds no open copy, and the University of Vienna's research portal refused the request; the author's preprint is posted only on ResearchGate and academia.edu, which this record does not use. What is said of it comes from summaries of its abstract returned by a search service, labelled unverified. A person could supply the chapter from the OUP volume or ask the author; a reading would move this to Active and should test whether its "corporate emotions" are corporate attitudes in List's sense. |
| [LIT-747](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-747.md) | Responsibility, Moral and Otherwise | Wolf (2015), Inquiry 58(2):127–142, the 2013 Routledge Lecture. The causal/moral contrast runs together two distinctions, shallow vs deep and moral vs nonmoral; we are deeply responsible for nonmoral traits and art too. Attributability and accountability are independent, not levels: accountability needs only wrongdoing, a position to know it, and its being up to the agent. The fit target of reactive attitudes is, tentatively, an "intelligent" self. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-565](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-565.md)): in full, from the author's typescript of the 2013 Routledge Lecture in Cambridge's Apollo repository. Worth reading as the only lawful full text by Wolf on responsibility the record holds. It argues that deep responsibility is not limited to the moral, and that attributability and accountability are independent, not two levels. Accountability may need nothing metaphysically robust. What makes a self a fit target of the reactive attitudes is, on her "hunch", that it is an "intelligent" self. Limits: the positive view is offered as a hunch, the psychopath is a stipulated case, and the lecture does not restate the Reason View of Freedom Within Reason ([LIT-685](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-685.md)). |
| [LIT-1001](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1001.md) v2 | Taken Out of Context: American Teen Sociality in Networked Publics | danah boyd (2008), PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. An ethnography of American teenagers on MySpace and Facebook. Networked publics have four properties (persistence, replicability, scalability, searchability) and three dynamics: invisible audiences, collapsed contexts, and the blurring of public and private. Collapsed contexts make it hard to keep distinct social contexts distinct. The analysis of self-presentation builds on Goffman (1959) and Meyrowitz (1985). | Active — read in part 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1432](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1432.md), Skimmed) from the author's copy at danah.org (www.danah.org/papers/TakenOutOfContext.pdf), licensed CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 (Appendix 3): Chapter 1 on networked publics, Chapter 4 on self-presentation and context, and Chapter 7 in full, with the passages on collapse elsewhere; Chapters 2, 3, 5 and 6 were not read in full. This extends the reading of 2026-10-12 ([NOTE-710](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-710.md)). Worth reading for its account of collapsed contexts: distinct social contexts are kept apart by spatial, social and temporal boundaries, and networked media remove them, so audiences a person keeps apart are brought together, often without the person seeing it. Its examples, after Meyrowitz (1985), show contradictory self-presentations doing no harm while the audiences stay segmented, and trouble when they meet. Read it knowing that the evidence is ethnographic, with no comparison of conflict between segmented and collapsed audiences, and that the teens' documented collisions are mostly one presentation misread by an unintended audience. |
| [LIT-1227](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1227.md) v2 | The Limits of the Self: Immunology and Biological Identity | Pradeu (2012). The immunological theory that an individual is defined by self and nonself fails, since immune responses to self and tolerance of foreign entities are the rule; Pradeu proposes a criterion of immunogenicity by discontinuity, and from it an immunological account of biological individuality. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-18, not read. A lawful full text was sought on 2026-10-29 and not reached. OpenAlex reports the book closed. The HAL record it lists, hal-01343696, is a notice with no file deposited (HAL API, 2026-10-29); its other location is an institutional e-book handle that needs a licence. Oxford Academic offers it only to subscribers, and web searches found reviews, paid e-books and Pradeu's earlier papers, not the book. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-1262](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1262.md) v2 | The free-energy self: A predictive coding account of self-recognition | Apps & Tsakiris (2014; online 2013), Neurosci. Biobehav. Rev. 41:85–97. Self-recognition is recast under the free-energy principle: one's own body is "the most likely to be 'me'", represented as a high-level, multimodal empirical prior learned from correlations between vision, touch, proprioception, corollary discharge and interoception, and "the notion that there is a 'self' is the most parsimonious and accurate explanation for sensory inputs". The rubber hand, enfacement and rubber-voice illusions become one effect: synchronous stimulation leaves surprise that multimodal areas explain away by raising the probability that the other hand, face or voice is "me" and lowering it for one's own. Context (a non-corporeal object, a misplaced hand, culture) acts as a prior. Three anatomical predictions are drawn: no unimodal area is self-specific; multimodal areas (TPJ, anterior insula, IPS, IFG) are engaged but not self-specific; predicted self-stimuli suppress activity. The authors concede there is "little direct evidence" for the account. | Active — read 2026-10-19 ([NOTE-991](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-991.md)) in full; worth reading as the first statement of the predictive-processing account of self-recognition and body ownership: one's own face, voice and body are recognised as "me" because a high-level, multimodal prior makes them the most probable cause of correlated input across the senses, and the rubber hand, enfacement and "rubber voice" illusions are that prior being updated when synchronous multisensory stimulation leaves surprise to explain away. Read it as a theoretical review that, by its authors' own account, rests on evidence that "neither largely supports nor refutes" it: no data, no model, no simulation, and predictions they call hard to falsify with standard fMRI. |
| [LIT-1263](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1263.md) v2 | Interoceptive inference, emotion, and the embodied self | Seth (2013), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 17(11):565–573, an Opinion article. Emotions are "interoceptive inference": felt states are the content of hierarchical top-down predictions of the causes of interoceptive signals, compared with bottom-up prediction errors in the anterior insula. Prediction errors are also cancelled by action, as descending predictions set the reference points of autonomic reflexes, the visceral counterpart of active inference in motor control. The same scheme is applied to the experience of body ownership. The rubber hand illusion is a revision of the multisensory self-model under precision-weighted error. Low interoceptive sensitivity goes with greater susceptibility to it, and a virtual hand pulsing in time with the heartbeat is owned more. No direct test of the model is claimed. | Active — read in full 2026-10-19 ([NOTE-1000](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1000.md)); worth reading as the short statement that put emotion and body ownership under one predictive-coding mechanism: felt emotion is the content of top-down predictions of the causes of interoceptive signals, the anterior insula is the comparator, and the experience of body ownership is what the brain infers to be "most likely to be me" from interoceptive and exteroceptive signals together. It is an opinion article with no new data. Its evidence is indirect and cited, and its one figure is a study by the author's own group, an augmented-reality rubber hand illusion whose virtual hand flashed in or out of time with the heartbeat. The record's bridge from its interoception cluster to body ownership. |
| [LIT-1264](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1264.md) | No specific relationship between hypnotic suggestibility and the rubber hand illusion | Ehrsson, Fotopoulou, Radziun, Longo & Tsakiris (2022), Nat Commun 13:564, a Matters Arising on Lush et al. (2020). Reanalysing the open data of all 353 participants, they find no relationship between hypnotisability and the synchronous-minus-asynchronous difference in illusion ratings (rho = -0.066, BF01 = 5.7) or in proprioceptive drift (rho = 0.047, BF01 = 1.7), a significant synchrony effect in every hypnotisability quartile, and no effect of explicit suggestions about which condition should work. The correlations Lush et al. report hold as much for the asynchronous condition and for an "impossible" visual hallucination item, so they read hypnotisability as a general influence on report, not a driver of the illusion. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-997](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-997.md)) in full with its supplementary figure; worth reading as the case for the rubber hand illusion surviving trait suggestibility, made from Lush et al.'s own open data (n = 353): the synchronous-minus-asynchronous difference in illusion ratings does not vary with hypnotisability (Bayes factor 5.7 for the null), is significant in every quartile of it including the least suggestible, and is unmoved by explicit instructions about which condition should work. Read it as a reanalysis and an argument, not new data: it treats the asynchronous condition as a valid control, which is exactly what the reply (Lush & Seth 2022) disputes, and its drift analysis is inconclusive by its own Bayes factor. |
| [LIT-1265](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1265.md) | Windows to the soul: Children and adults see the eyes as the location of the self | Starmans & Bloom (2012), Cognition 123(2):313–318. Three experiments with 4- and 5-year-olds (41–50 per study) and US adults on Mechanical Turk (51–53 per study) asked which of two pictured flies or snowflakes was "closer to" a cartoon character. Both groups chose positions near the eyes: over the lower body on a girl; at the chest on an alien whose eyes were there; and in front of the eyes over behind the head, or in front of the feet, on a profile. The authors conclude that people intuitively think of the self as located at or near the eyes, and, since preschoolers share it, that this is not learned from ideas about the brain. The judgement is about another, drawn person, and the step from "closer to her" to "the location of the self" is assumed, not tested. | Active — read in full 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-995](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-995.md)), from the published article on the authors' lab site at Yale; worth reading as the best-known folk-judgement study of where a person is in their body, and for what such a study can and cannot show. Preschoolers and adults on Mechanical Turk chose which of two pictures had a fly, or a snowflake, closer to a cartoon character. They chose positions near the eyes: on a girl, near the eyes over the body; on an alien with its eyes on its chest, near the chest-eyes; on a profile, in front of the eyes over behind the head and over places the character could see. The authors conclude that children and adults intuitively place the self at or near the eyes. Read it as a judgement about where another, drawn, person is, with small samples, some slips in the statistics and an inference from "closer to Mary" to "the location of the self" that the design assumes. It bears on none of the rubber hand THEORYs. |
| [LIT-1266](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1266.md) | Where exactly am I? Self-location judgements distribute between head and torso | Alsmith & Longo (2014), Consciousness and Cognition 24:70–74. Ten adults set a pointer, rotating in their sagittal plane, to point "directly at you", by hand while blindfolded or by telling the experimenter when to stop it. Responses clustered on the upper face and the upper torso, and the starting position of the pointer decided which: from above, the face; from below, the torso. Vision and touch gave the same pattern. The authors conclude that the self is judged neither spread over the body nor at one point, and that the concept of the self as a spatial entity is "inherently ambiguous". Small sample, 20.7% of trials lost, and a reanalysis whose key effect is misreported. | Active — read in full 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1008](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1008.md)), from the published article on the second author's lab site; worth reading as the first study that asks people to point at themselves on their own body, rather than on a drawing or a cartoon, and as a measure of self-location that is neither a questionnaire nor a walking-back drift. Ten adults, standing, set a pointer rotating in front of them so that it pointed "directly at you", blindfolded by hand or by telling the experimenter when to stop it. Answers fell mostly on two regions, the upper face and the upper torso, and which one depended on where the pointer started: from above, the face; from below, the torso. Seeing and touching gave the same pattern, the touch version less sharply. Read it as a small pilot with a fifth of its trials lost to a camera fault, whose re-analysis without the lower torso misreports a non-significant effect as significant, and whose result may reflect where the pointer reached first as much as where people feel they are. It bears on [THEORY-768](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-768.md)'s self-location dimension; it bears on none of the rubber hand THEORYs. |
| [LIT-1267](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1267.md) | Reply to: No specific relationship between hypnotic suggestibility and the rubber hand illusion | Lush & Seth (2022), Nat Commun 13:563, replying to Ehrsson et al. (2022). They accept the reanalyses and dispute the reading: an asynchronous condition is no control for demand characteristics, because expectancies are higher for the synchronous condition, and in their sample the expectancy difference did not vary with hypnotisability (b = -0.16, P = 0.072, B = 0.07). Highly hypnotisable participants may meet those expectancies by generating the experience, less hypnotisable ones by response bias. Agreement with "I felt as if the rubber hand were my hand" rose with hypnotisability (b = 0.76, rs = 0.27) and averaged 0.7 on a seven-point scale whose maximum is 3. Whether multisensory integration plays a significant role in RHI measures awaits experiments with adequate controls. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1003](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1003.md)) in full; worth reading as the clearest short statement of why a synchronous-minus-asynchronous difference cannot by itself show that the rubber hand illusion is multisensory: participants expect more from the synchronous condition, and in Lush et al.'s sample (n = 353) that expectancy difference did not vary with hypnotisability, so a null relation between hypnotisability and the synchrony effect is what demand characteristics predict too. It adds that agreement with the ownership item rises steeply with hypnotisability (b = 0.76 per SWASH point) and reaches minimal agreement only in the top 31%. Read it as a reply: the expectancy and ownership regressions are post hoc, as the authors grant of both sides, and its alternative for low-suggestible participants, response bias, is asserted and not measured. |
| [LIT-1268](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1268.md) | No causal link between changes in hand position sense and feeling of limb ownership in the rubber hand illusion | Abdulkarim & Ehrsson (2016; online 2015), Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics 78:707–720. During 90 s of synchronous or asynchronous brushing, a motor moved the participant's hidden hand 8 cm toward or away from the rubber hand at 0.9 mm/s, below the threshold for feeling the movement. Pointing to the hand followed the displacement (drift main effect η² .68 in Experiment 1), but questionnaire ownership depended only on synchrony and did not differ between toward, away or a static hand (n = 18 in each of two experiments). The static condition reproduced the classic synchronous drift and its correlation with the illusion (r = .56). The authors conclude that changing hand position sense does not change ownership, so drift is not a cause of the illusion; whether ownership causes drift is left open. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-992](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-992.md)) in full; worth reading as the direct test of whether a change in felt hand position causes the feeling of owning the rubber hand. A motor slid the hidden real hand 8 cm toward or away from the rubber hand during stroking, too slowly to notice; pointing moved with it by about 5–6 cm, and questionnaire ownership did not change, in two experiments of 18. The authors conclude that drift is not a prerequisite of the illusion and is a process distinct from ownership, while still defending drift as a measure when the hand is immobile. Read it as a null result from 18 participants with no equivalence test, within distances (8–24 cm) where the illusion is known to work, and with some statistics that do not agree with their own test values. |
| [LIT-1271](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1271.md) | Trait phenomenological control predicts experience of mirror synaesthesia and the rubber hand illusion | Lush, Botan, Scott, Seth, Ward & Dienes (2020), Nature Communications 11:4853. Trait hypnotisability (the Sussex-Waterloo Scale, SWASH), which the authors call phenomenological control, predicted vicarious pain (n = 404) and mirror touch (n = 154), and, in a rubber hand illusion study of 353, agreement with the ownership and location items after both synchronous and asynchronous brushing, a visual control item, and, weakly, synchronous proprioceptive drift. An attempt to manipulate expectations failed, so the evidence is correlational. The authors conclude that the usual asynchrony and control-item checks do not rule out suggestion, and that the illusion as commonly reported may be at least partly an implicit imaginative-suggestion effect. | Active — read in full 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-990](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-990.md)), with its supplementary information and the peer review file; worth reading as the first large-sample test of whether the rubber hand illusion, as it is usually measured, tracks the trait that hypnosis scales measure. In 353 undergraduates, hypnotisability predicted agreement with the ownership items after synchronous brushing (about half a scale point per SWASH point, rs 0.26), and just as well after asynchronous brushing and for a visual "control" item; it predicted synchronous proprioceptive drift weakly (rs 0.11). In separate samples of 404 and 154 it predicted vicarious pain and mirror touch. The planned manipulation of expectations failed, so nothing here is causal, and the pre-registered test, hypnotisability against the synchronous-minus-asynchronous difference, was inconclusive. Read it as strong evidence that the standard asynchrony and control-item checks do not control for suggestion, and as no evidence on whether the synchrony effect survives such a control. Seth, author of [LIT-1263](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1263.md), is a co-author. |
| [LIT-1272](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1272.md) | Explaining Away the Body: Experiences of Supernaturally Caused Touch and Touch on Non-Hand Objects within the Rubber Hand Illusion | Hohwy & Paton (2010), PLoS ONE 5:e9416. Through a head-mounted display, a foreign arm (an experimenter's, then a rubber one) was seen aligned with the participant's own arm while both were tapped. Synchronous tapping, against asynchronous, raised ratings that the felt touch was produced by the seen finger on the seen arm, and the rating held through pauses of up to a minute (n = 13). After onset, synchrony also raised ratings that a finger hovering 5 cm off the rubber arm caused the touch and that touch was felt on a cardboard box (n = 11 and 10); without prior onset the box gave no synchrony difference (n = 9). The real hand was 0.13 °C cooler under synchrony in one comparison only. The authors read the results as the visual body image being "explained away" by ongoing multisensory inference, and as support for one-deficit theories of delusion. | Active — read in full 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-998](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-998.md)); worth reading as a philosopher's small rubber hand experiment that pushes the illusion past where it should break, and as the study Apps & Tsakiris cite for cooling of the real hand. Through a head-mounted display the foreign arm was seen exactly where the participant's own arm lay. Synchronous tapping made people rate the touch as produced on the seen arm (13 people), and after onset they went on to rate touch as caused by a finger hovering 5 cm off a rubber arm, or felt on a cardboard box (10 and 11 people); some described the hovering finger as magnetism, ESP or black magic. Nine people shown the box without prior onset gave no synchrony difference. The real hand was 0.13 °C cooler under synchrony in one of four comparisons, by what reads as a one-tailed test. Read it as four small samples, single leading questions with no ownership item, no expectation measure, and a temperature result too weak to carry the claim that the real hand loses ownership. |
| [LIT-1273](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1273.md) | Moving a Rubber Hand that Feels Like Your Own: A Dissociation of Ownership and Agency | Kalckert & Ehrsson (2012), Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 6:40. A moving rubber hand illusion: the participant taps a hidden index finger linked by a rod to the finger of a wooden model hand in view. Synchronous movement gave ownership (mean 1.63 on −3 to +3) and agency (2.44), and a 1.73 cm drift toward the model, where a ~500 ms asynchrony gave neither (n = 20 and 20). In a 2 × 2 design (n = 32 each), passive movement abolished agency (−0.61) but left ownership (1.57) and drift, and a model hand rotated 180° abolished ownership (−0.62) and drift but left agency (2.2): a double dissociation on questionnaires. Agency was higher, and correlated with ownership (r = 0.50), only when the hand was owned. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-993](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-993.md)) in full; worth reading as the first experiment to set the sense of ownership and the sense of agency against each other in one rubber hand paradigm. A wooden model hand whose index finger is linked by a rod to the participant's hidden finger is owned when it moves in time with the real finger, whether the movement is the participant's own or imposed by the experimenter, and is controlled when the participant moves, whether or not it is owned: passive movement removed agency and left ownership, and rotating the model hand 180° removed ownership and left agency. Read it as 104 participants over four between-group experiments, with named non-parametric tests, means and SDs but no standardised effect sizes, a dissociation shown on questionnaires alone (drift measures ownership only), and no control for what participants expected the conditions to do. It also finds the two not independent: agency was rated higher, and correlated with ownership, only when the hand was owned. |
| [LIT-1274](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1274.md) v2 | Full-body illusions and minimal phenomenal selfhood | Blanke & Metzinger (2009), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 13(1):7–13. An opinion piece proposing that research on bodily self-consciousness isolate minimal phenomenal selfhood (MPS), "the conscious experience of being a self", defined by three dimensions: global self-identification with the body, spatiotemporal self-location, and a weak (geometrical) first-person perspective, claimed jointly necessary and sufficient. The rubber-hand illusion and somatoparaphrenia alter only partial ownership and so do not touch MPS; out-of-body experience, heautoscopy and the full-body illusions of Lenggenhager et al. and Ehrsson (2007) do. Agency is causally enabling for MPS but not constitutive of it. | Active — read 2026-10-19 ([NOTE-1002](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1002.md)) in full; worth reading as the short programmatic paper that names minimal phenomenal selfhood (MPS), the simplest form of the experience of being a self, and splits it into three dimensions: self-identification with the body as a whole, self-location, and a weak, purely geometrical first-person perspective. Its distinctive move is to set partial ownership (the rubber-hand illusion, somatoparaphrenia) apart from global ownership, and to say only the second reaches MPS, so that full-body illusions and neurological out-of-body phenomena, not the rubber hand, are the entry point. Its most quotable thesis is that bodily agency "is a causally enabling, but not a constitutive condition, for phenomenal selfhood". An opinion piece: no new data, the evidence cited, and the necessity and sufficiency claims asserted. |
| [LIT-1275](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1275.md) | What is embodiment? A psychometric approach | Longo, Schüür, Kammers, Tsakiris & Haggard (2008), Cognition 107:978–998. 131 participants rated 27 statements after synchronous and asynchronous brushing of a rubber hand. Principal components analysis gave four components in both conditions (embodiment of the rubber hand, loss of own hand, movement, affect) and a fifth, deafference, after asynchrony only. A second analysis split embodiment into ownership, location and agency. Ownership and location were positive after synchronous brushing and negative after asynchronous; agency was negative after both. Drift toward the rubber hand was 1.34 cm after synchrony and a non-significant 0.30 cm after asynchrony, and ownership and location each predicted it. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1004](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1004.md)) in full, from the published article on the first author's lab site; worth reading as the first large-sample measurement of what the rubber hand illusion feels like, and as the study that split "embodiment" of a rubber hand into ownership, location and agency. 131 people rated 27 statements after 60 s of synchronous and of asynchronous brushing. A principal components analysis found four components in both conditions (embodiment of the rubber hand, loss of own hand, movement, affect) and a fifth, deafference, only after asynchronous brushing. Ownership and location rose above neutral only after synchrony, agency stayed below it, and ownership and location each predicted proprioceptive drift. Read it knowing that the three subcomponents come from a second varimax rotation of ten items dominated by one component, that there is no control for expectation or suggestion, and that every item is about a hand, none about the whole body. |
| [LIT-1276](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1276.md) | Demand Characteristics Confound the Rubber Hand Illusion | Lush (2020), Collabra: Psychology 6(1):22. A pre-registered quasi-experiment on the controls of the rubber hand illusion. Twenty undergraduates (after 12 pre-registered exclusions) who had never taken part in it were shown a text and a video of the procedure and rated how far they expected to feel each of Botvinick & Cohen's three illusion and six control statements, under synchronous and asynchronous brushing. Expectancy was higher for illusion than control statements under synchrony (M 1.7 against 0.0, t(19) = 6.24, d = 1.40) and for synchronous than asynchronous illusion statements (1.7 against 0.4, t(19) = 4.68, d = 1.05), and nine who had never heard of the illusion showed the same. The controls therefore do not match expectations, and the author concludes the illusion "may be, partially or entirely, a suggestion effect"; he proposes controls matched on expectancy and on suggestion difficulty. | Active — read in full 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1005](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1005.md)) from the author's final manuscript on PsyArXiv; worth reading as the direct test of the assumption behind every standard check on the rubber hand illusion, that expectations are matched between the "illusion" and "control" statements and between synchronous and asynchronous brushing. Twenty people who never underwent the illusion read a description of it, watched a 62-second video and rated, for each of Botvinick & Cohen's nine statements, how far they expected to feel it. They expected the illusion statements more than the control statements under synchrony (1.7 against 0.0, d = 1.40) and the illusion statements more under synchrony than asynchrony (1.7 against 0.4, d = 1.05): the pattern published reports show. Read it as showing that the usual controls cannot rule out suggestion, not as showing that the illusion is suggestion; the author says so. | [LIT-1277](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1277.md) v4 | Rubber hands 'feel' touch that eyes see | Botvinick & Cohen (1998), Nature 391:756. Ten subjects watched a rubber left hand being brushed in synchrony with their own hidden left hand. After ten minutes they affirmed feeling the touch where they saw the rubber hand touched, that the touch was caused by the brush on the rubber hand, and that the rubber hand was theirs. After a 30-minute exposure, blind reaches toward the real hand were displaced toward the rubber hand in proportion to how long the illusion was reported, and an asynchronously brushed control group reported the illusion for 7% of the time against 42% and showed no drift toward it. The authors conclude that intermodal matching "can be sufficient for self-attribution". | Active — read 2026-10-19 ([NOTE-1006](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1006.md)) in full; worth reading as the one-page report that founded the rubber hand illusion paradigm: synchronous brushing of a seen rubber hand and the hidden real hand makes touch be felt where the rubber hand is touched and the rubber hand be felt as one's own, and after 30 minutes the felt position of the real hand drifts toward the rubber hand in proportion to how long the illusion lasted, while asynchronous brushing abolishes both. Read it as a brief communication: ten subjects, no stated control-group size, statistics given only as P-values, and a connectionist model and a premotor-cell analogy mentioned but not shown. Its closing claim, that intermodal matching "can be sufficient for self-attribution", is the sentence the later literature on body ownership builds on. |
| [LIT-1279](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1279.md) v2 | Video Ergo Sum: Manipulating Bodily Self-Consciousness | Lenggenhager, Tadi, Metzinger & Blanke (2007), Science 317:1096–1099. A whole-body rubber hand illusion in video virtual reality. Participants saw their own back, filmed from 2 m behind, as a body standing in front of them, stroked in or out of time with strokes on their real back. Under synchronous stroking they rated the seen body as theirs and, after blindfolded displacement, returned to a point shifted toward it (24.1 cm in study I, n = 14). In study II (n = 14) a mannequin gave the same, and a non-bodily object a weaker, non-significant drift with no self-identification. Nobody reported disembodiment or a shifted viewpoint. The authors conclude that self-location and the global ownership they tie to selfhood rest partly on the same visuo-tactile integration as body-part ownership, constrained by knowledge of what a body looks like. | Active — read in full 2026-10-19 ([NOTE-999](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-999.md)), with its supporting online material and the 2008 e-letter exchange; worth reading as the first full-body version of the rubber hand illusion and the experiment the self-model theory cites for global body ownership. Two groups of 14 people saw, through a head-mounted display, a video of a body 2 m in front of them being stroked on the back. When the stroking was synchronous with strokes on their own back, they rated the seen body as theirs and, displaced blindfolded, walked back to a spot about 17 to 25 cm toward it. A mannequin worked; a rectangular object weakened the drift and was not felt as one's body. Nobody reported leaving the body or seeing from elsewhere, so the authors call it heautoscopy-like, not an out-of-body experience. Read it as two small samples with modest, partly inconsistent effects, and with a rival reading (self-recognition in a video system) that its critics raised and its design does not exclude. |
