A resampling study of the synchronous-condition reports of 351 participants from Lush et al. 2020, run as 10,000 simulated experiments of 20 participants each. Unselected samples found mean agreement with the three standard statements significantly above zero in 83% of experiments; samples from above the median of hypnotisability (subjective SWASH) in 99%; from below it in 51%. For the ownership statement alone the lower half gave significant agreement in about 4% of experiments, and the upper half in 74% (supplement). The authors argue that the relationship is not too small to matter, that the synchronous–asynchronous difference cannot be interpreted because of Lush (2020), and that implicit, neuroimaging and animal measures are tied to ownership only through these reports. | Active — read in full 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1001](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1001.md)) from the accepted manuscript on PsyArXiv, with the authors' analysis notebooks for 10, 20 and 50 participants; worth reading as the clearest demonstration of what a modest correlation between hypnotisability and rubber hand report does to a field of small studies. Resampling the 351 synchronous-condition reports of Lush et al. 2020 in simulated experiments of 20, samples drawn from the upper half of the hypnotisability scale found significant agreement with the three illusion statements 99% of the time and samples from the lower half 51%; for the one ownership statement, "I felt as if the rubber hand were my hand", the figures were 74% and 4%. Read it as a reanalysis of one dataset, with no new data and no asynchronous or drift analysis. Its headline numbers depend on n = 20: at n = 50 the lower half finds the averaged illusion statements in 95% of experiments, though the ownership statement still only in 6%. The authors themselves leave open that the same people may have the illusion for other reasons. |
| [LIT-1281](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1281.md) | The Rubber Hand Illusion: Feeling of Ownership and Proprioceptive Drift Do Not Go Hand in Hand | Rohde, Di Luca & Ernst (2011), PLoS ONE 6:e21659. Robot arms stroked a rubber hand and the hidden real hand, and felt finger position was probed by a projected dot. Drift toward the rubber hand built up to about 5–6 cm under synchronous stroking, and to the same level when the hand was only seen, unstroked, or when asynchronous stroking was interrupted every 10 s for measurement. Only 120 s of continuous asynchronous stroking held drift near zero (about 1 cm), which reproduces the classic synchronous–asynchronous difference. The questionnaire showed ownership only after synchronous stroking. The authors conclude that drift and ownership come from different integration processes, that asynchrony suppresses drift rather than synchrony causing it, and that drift is not a valid proxy for ownership. Groups were of ten. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1009](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1009.md)) in full; worth reading as the study that broke the assumed tie between proprioceptive drift and the feeling of owning the rubber hand. With robot-delivered stroking and a visual probe of felt finger position, drift toward the rubber hand appeared under synchronous stroking, under no stroking at all (only seeing the hand), and under asynchronous stroking interrupted every 10 s, at levels not significantly different from synchronous stroking (about 5–6 cm); only continuous asynchronous stroking kept it near zero. Ownership, by questionnaire, needed synchrony. The authors conclude that drift comes from visuo-proprioceptive integration that asynchrony suppresses, and that "conclusions about feelings of ownership cannot be drawn from measuring proprioceptive drift alone". Read it as groups of 10, a visual-judgement measure rather than reaching, and an Experiment 2 whose ownership evidence is anecdotal debriefing, not a questionnaire. |
| [LIT-1360](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1360.md) v2 | Real patterns, the predictive mind, and the cognitive construction of the manifest image | Gładziejewski (2025), Synthese 206:225. Dennett's compression criterion for real patterns is carried through minimum description length, Bayesian inference and variational free energy, so learning a generative model is real-pattern extraction from sensory data. The manifest image is then a structural description of the sensory signal, equally veridical for an envatted twin with matched input. Applied to selves: a self-model compresses self-generated regularities by positing one common cause, real as a pattern, not as a substance, and the realism dispute is over criteria. Applied to objects: compression-based composition (Bird 2023) favours cats over arbitrary sums. | Active — read in full 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1056](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1056.md)) from the publisher's open-access PDF (Springer, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); worth reading as a clear derivation of Dennett's real patterns into predictive processing, through minimum description length and the complexity–accuracy split of free energy, and as a short diagnosis of the realism dispute about selves: a self-model compresses self-generated regularities by positing one common cause, so the self is real as a pattern and not as a substance, and the dispute is over criteria. The structural, Kantian realism it draws (the manifest image is veridical in a matched vat) needs manifest content to be wholly structural, which it assumes. It says nothing about consciousness, and it does not say a self-model exaggerates the self's unity. |
| [LIT-1368](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1368.md) v2 | Prominent and persistent loss of past awareness in amnesia: Delusion, impaired consciousness or coping strategy? | Wilson, Kopelman and Kapur (2008). On Clive Wearing's repeated claims, in his diary and in speech, that he has just become conscious for the first time, and his denial of earlier awareness when shown evidence of it; the paper weighs whether this is delusion, impaired consciousness or a coping strategy. | Unavailable — no lawful copy reached, 2026-10-22; failed on availability, as far as could be told. The article is closed: Unpaywall and OpenAlex report no open copy and no repository full text. OpenAlex lists two repository records: King's College London's Pure page (abstract only, no file) and the University of Southampton's ePrints record 55417, which could not be opened past its bot check, so whether it holds a file is unknown. The MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit record has no file. The abstract, read from the King's College record, confirms the summary. Registered from the owner's exchange of 2026-10-22, "Graph Learning Applications". No NOTE is filed. |
| [LIT-1369](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1369.md) v2 | Dense amnesia in a professional musician following herpes simplex virus encephalitis | Wilson, Baddeley and Kapur (1995). The case study of the musician Clive Wearing after herpes simplex encephalitis in 1985: very dense anterograde amnesia and extensive retrograde amnesia, with musical performance (playing, sight-reading, conducting) largely preserved. | Unavailable — no lawful copy reached, 2026-10-22; failed on availability. The article is closed: Unpaywall and OpenAlex report no open copy and no repository full text, Taylor & Francis offers it only behind a paywall, PubMed (8557808) has the abstract only, the MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit bibliography lists it without a file, and a web search found no author's or institutional copy. The abstract, read from PubMed, confirms the dense amnesia but does not mention preserved musical skill, and says the patient's belief that he has just woken "appears to be the result of a delusion rather than the consequence of his amnesia". Registered from the owner's exchange of 2026-10-22, "Graph Learning Applications". No NOTE is filed. |
| [LIT-1379](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1379.md) v2 | Human Nature and the Social Order | Cooley (1902). Argues that society and the individual are two aspects of one life and that the immediate social reality is the idea people have of one another. The self of common speech is a feeling of appropriation attached to ideas formed in communication, and in "a very large and interesting class of cases" it is the "looking-glass self": an imagined appearance in another mind, an imagined judgement of it, and a self-feeling such as pride or mortification. | Active — skimmed 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1080](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1080.md)): five of twelve chapters (I, III, V, VI, VIII) read in full from the Project Gutenberg text of the 1902 edition (public domain); worth reading for the source of the looking-glass self and for how much of the imagined-audience argument it already holds: the other in whose mind one sees oneself is imagined and may be absent, dead or ideal, a group is realized as imagined persons, conformity is driven by a judgement one attributes to others, and opposition to what others enjoin is itself steered by it. The looking-glass self is one large class of the social self, not its definition. An essay from introspection, two children and literature, with no method that could fail. |
| [LIT-1394](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1394.md) v2 | The Way I Am | Eminem (2000), from The Marshall Mathers LP. The couplet the record cites, "I am whatever you say I am" and "If I wasn't then why would I say I am", is delivered amid complaints about fame, fans and expectations, and reads as defiance, not assent. Its second line is taken from Eric B. & Rakim's "As the Rhyme Goes On". | Unfetched — filed 2026-10-22, not studied as a text, and on 2026-10-29 not heard. The work is a recording, so a reading of it is a listening. A lawful free copy is at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mQvteoFiMlg, the official video on the EminemVEVO channel, titled "Eminem - The Way I Am (Clean Version)", which Wikipedia's article links and YouTube's oEmbed confirmed on 2026-10-29. This client cannot listen to audio or watch video, so it is Unfetched ([ADR-053](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-053.md)). The record holds no licensed lyric text, and lyric pages on unlicensed sites were not used. Listening, to the clean edit or to the album track on a licensed service, would check the couplet [CLAIM-415](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-415.md) quotes and the context the summary gives; the clean edit may mute words elsewhere. No NOTE is filed. |
| [LIT-1398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1398.md) v3 | The Self-Fulfilling Prophecy | Merton (1948). Names the self-fulfilling prophecy: a false definition of a situation evokes behaviour that makes the originally false conception come true, and the prophet then cites the course of events as proof that he was right from the beginning. Builds on the Thomas theorem, that situations defined as real are real in their consequences. Applies it to American ethnic and racial prejudice, sets beside it "moral alchemy", in which the in-group renames the same conduct as virtue in itself and vice in an out-group, and argues that institutional change, not education, breaks the circle. | Active — read 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1409](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1409.md)) in full, from a JSTOR download of the article posted on a course wiki (https://entrepreneurscommunicate.pbworks.com/f/Merton.%2BSelf%2BFulfilling%2BProfecy.pdf); worth reading as the essay that names the self-fulfilling prophecy and defines it, and that sets beside it a second route, "moral alchemy", by which an out-group is condemned whatever it does. Read it knowing that it is a magazine essay on American race relations in 1948, with no references and no sources for its figures, that it sets the self-defeating ("suicidal") prophecy aside in a footnote, and that two of its three opening examples are forecasts, not false definitions of a present situation. |
| [LIT-1410](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1410.md) v3 | Telling More Than We Can Know: Verbal Reports on Mental Processes | Nisbett & Wilson (1977). Reviews evidence that people may have little or no direct introspective access to higher-order cognitive processes: they can be unaware of a stimulus that influenced a response, of the response, or of the influence. Reports on one's own processes rest on a priori, implicit causal theories about what plausibly caused what, so they are accurate when the influential stimulus is salient and a plausible cause, and not otherwise. Its test is that observers given only a description of the situation predict the same effects the subjects report. | Active — read 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1412](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1412.md)) in full, from a scan of the published article in an MIT course-readings folder (https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/15341_Readings/Social_Cognition/Nisbett_Wilson_1977_Telling_more_than_we_can_know.pdf); worth reading as the review, with eight small studies of its own, that people's reports of why they responded as they did miss effective stimuli and credit ineffective ones, and match what observers predict from a description alone, so that they come from causal theories, not from access to the process. Read it knowing that its situations were chosen to produce error, that several of its own studies are reported briefly or unpublished, that it is about the influence of stimuli on responses, not about attributions of agency, and that it shows only that such access as exists does no better than an observer, not that there is none. |
| [LIT-1417](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1417.md) v2 | Failure to Detect Mismatches Between Intention and Outcome in a Simple Decision Task | Johansson, Hall, Sikström & Olsson (2005). 120 participants chose the more attractive of two female faces; on three of 15 trials a card trick handed them the face they had rejected. Only 13% of the 354 swapped trials were detected at the time, at most 26% counting every later form of detection, whatever the faces' similarity or the time allowed. Reasons given for the rejected face matched reasons for real choices in length, emotionality, specificity and certainty, and some named features only the rejected face had. The authors call this choice blindness. | Active — read 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1398](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1398.md)) in full, with its Supporting Online Material, from the authors' posting of the final published version on the Lund University Cognitive Science site; worth reading as the experiment that catches a person giving reasons for a choice they did not make: 13% of 354 covertly swapped outcomes were noticed at the time, and the reasons given for the swapped face matched reasons for real choices on every measure but one. Read it knowing that it is one low-stakes task (attractiveness of unfamiliar faces), that detection was counted from spontaneous report by design, that the report comparison is a null on eight coded variables, and that it does not show ordinary reasons to be confabulated, which the authors leave open. |
| [LIT-1677](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1677.md) | A comparison of minimal group induction procedures | Two small experiments with US undergraduates (N = 42 and 73) compare four ways of making minimal groups. In the classic one, participants are falsely told their painting preferences put them in a group. In the others, they imagine being assigned, are assigned at random, or only memorize five names from one group, with no categorization at all. On explicit liking and identification, and on a bonus-money allocation between two other participants, all four produced comparable in-group favouritism. On IATs of attitude (pleasant/unpleasant) and identification (self/other), only memorization produced large effects; the classic procedure produced none. Implicit and explicit favouritism correlated weakly. Explicit identification correlated with allocation favouritism (r = .37). The allocation result was carried mostly by one of the two colour groups. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1319](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1319.md)), in place of [LIT-1697](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1697.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as a direct test of how little it takes to make a minimal group. Merely studying a group's names ties it to "self" on an implicit measure, and imagined or random assignment yields the same explicit favouritism as the classic procedure. Read in place of Tajfel et al. 1971 ([LIT-1697](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1697.md), Unavailable); small samples, one college. |
| [LIT-1685](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1685.md) | Trauma, prejudice, large-group identity and psychoanalysis | A memorial lecture, not a study. Volkan defines a large group as thousands or millions of people who mostly never meet but share sentiments, and pictures large-group identity as a tent's canvas worn over each member's individual identity, with the leader as its pole. Membership in ethnic, national and religious groups begins in childhood, through identification with parents' investment in the group and the images and "ego tasks" they deposit in the child; after adolescence a core large-group identity cannot be changed. From unofficial dialogues between conflicting groups (1980s to early 2000s), he reports that the central psychological factor in large-group conflict is the need to protect large-group identity, and that a participant who felt that identity threatened would speak with emotion of an injury suffered by ancestors centuries before. The shared image of such an event, "real, fantasized or even mythologized", undergoes a change of function as it passes down the generations and becomes an identity marker: a chosen trauma. Chosen traumas feed entitlement ideologies and, in a "time collapse", make the old event feel recent, as Milošević did with Kosovo 1389, with dehumanization and purification following. Recent traumas, the Holocaust among them, are not chosen traumas but undigested ones, bound up with large-group mourning. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1250](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1250.md)), in place of [LIT-1727](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1727.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as Volkan's late, short restatement of chosen trauma, its trigger in threatened identity and its distinction from the mourning of recent trauma, read in place of his 2001 paper; the evidence is his own clinical and diplomatic observation, without method or measure. |
| [LIT-1687](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1687.md) | Two Decades of Terror Management Theory: A Meta-Analysis of Mortality Salience Research | Burke, Martens & Faucher (2010). A meta-analysis of experiments testing terror management theory's mortality salience hypothesis: reminding people of their own death increases defence of their cultural worldview and the pursuit of self-esteem, with a moderate effect across many paradigms and moderators such as delay. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Many Labs 4 (Klein et al. 2022) ([LIT-1796](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1796.md)) and Chen et al. 2025 ([LIT-1730](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1730.md)). |
| [LIT-1689](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1689.md) | The Concept and Psychological Consequences of Symbolic Immortality | An ANU master's thesis in psychology testing Otto Rank's idea that people need to feel they will transcend death, in three modes (children, an afterlife, creative work), to which Lifton added two (nature and experiential transcendence, an expansion of the self). It reviews ethnographic, ancient and modern evidence that all five modes are expressed. Then it surveys 440 Australian adults aged 18 to 88, recruited through Christian, Yoga, Spiritualist and secular groups, using vignettes rated as imagined consolation in terminal illness. Having a mode in one's life and religious affiliation predict accepting it; education predicts accepting the modes less. The modes predict personality only weakly; Rank's links to neuroticism and to sex differences fail. | Active — skimmed 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1312](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1312.md)), in place of [LIT-1714](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1714.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as a review of how Rank's and Lifton's modes were measured by 1991, and as one survey showing that the secular modes go with accepting death as final. It is a modest test that found little; skim chapters 1, 4 and 10. |
| [LIT-1690](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1690.md) | Group-level emotions | A short review of intergroup emotions theory by its founders. When people self-categorize as group members, the group becomes an aspect of the self and events are appraised for what they mean to the group; the resulting emotions are felt on the group's behalf. Which emotions are felt shifts with the salient membership; members converge on a group norm for them; they need no personal involvement (guilt for others' misdeeds); and identification moderates them, the highly identified sometimes reappraising to avoid negative group emotions. Such emotions predict collective action and treatment of out-groups (contempt more than anger predicts extreme violence) and of the in-group, and they can be regulated, which suggests interventions in intractable conflicts. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1285](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1285.md)), in place of [LIT-1722](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1722.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the founders' compact statement that an identified-with group is appraised as part of the self, with self-categorization and identification kept apart. |
| [LIT-1699](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1699.md) | Pair-Bonding as Inclusion of Other in the Self: A Literature Review | A five-page review, by Aron's group, of research on the self-expansion model's principle of inclusion of other in the self (IOS) in long-term romantic relationships. In a close relationship each partner treats the other's resources, perspectives and identities as to some extent their own (Aron et al. 1991). The single-item IOS circle scale is the standard measure. It tracks feeling and behaving close and correlates with cognitive signs of inclusion, such as slower self-trait judgements where the partner differs and self–partner confusions in memory. Studies since 2013 link greater overlap to self-like treatment of the partner: comparisons, pain and sleep, and honour-based aggression. They also add a two-dimensional model of relational self-change and a perceived-inclusion construct. No new data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1276](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1276.md)), in place of [LIT-1706](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1706.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as a current map of what the IOS scale is used for and validated against. Its account of Aron et al. 1991 is two sentences. |
| [LIT-1702](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1702.md) | Future self-continuity: how conceptions of the future self transform intertemporal choice | Hershfield (2011). A review, mostly of the author's own studies, of "future self-continuity": following Parfit, people who feel their future self is less connected to them treat it more like a stranger and save less for it. Three components are proposed. Similarity, measured by choosing overlapping circles (adapted from Aron et al.'s inclusion-of-other-in-self scale) for one's self in ten years, predicted patient choices and accumulated assets, controlling for age; neural activity for the future self that looked more like activity for another person predicted steeper discounting (r = .47). Vividness: seeing an age-progressed image of oneself raised hypothetical retirement saving. Positivity: respect for the elderly tracked national saving rates and, when induced, raised patient choices. Asking directly how much people liked and cared for their future selves did not predict choice, though those answers were near ceiling. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1259](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1259.md)) from the NIH author manuscript (PMC3764505), served by NCBI's PMC OAI-PMH service after Europe PMC refused this client; worth reading as the short statement of the future self-continuity programme, and as the record's clearest case of a measured extent of the self predicting concern-like behaviour where directly reported caring did not. Read it knowing that the review gives almost no statistics, that the caring null comes from a ceiling, and that the circles are framed as similarity. |
| [LIT-1703](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1703.md) | Culture and the self: Implications for cognition, emotion, and motivation | Markus & Kitayama (1991). A theoretical review. Cultures differ in how they construe the self. The independent construal, most clearly American and western European, is a bounded self defined by internal attributes. The interdependent construal, found in Japan and other Asian cultures but also in African, Latin American, Hindu and southern European ones, is a self defined by relationships with specific others in specific contexts: "others are included within the boundaries of the self" (p. 245), though it "does not result in a merging of self and other" (p. 228). The authors predict, and review evidence, that interdependent selves know more about others and describe themselves by context. They expect them to feel and express "other-focused" emotions (shame, sympathy, amae) more and "ego-focused" ones (anger, pride) less. They expect them to pursue achievement for others and to show modesty, not self-enhancement. They name a third option between selfishness and selflessness: "a self defined in relationship to others" (p. 247). | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1275](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1275.md)) from the published APA scan posted by Markus on her own website (hazelmarkus.com/research); worth reading as the classic statement that cultures construe the self as more or less inclusive of others. For the owner's thesis ([CLAIM-491](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-491.md)) it supports the premise, a self that includes others, and names the thesis's middle term, "an alternative to selfishness … besides selflessness" (p. 247). It does not support the step to self-interest: the authors deny merging and allow "genuine, other-oriented, altruistic" motives. The evidence is mostly cross-national contrasts, often second-hand or unpublished, with culture standing in for an unmeasured construal. |
| [LIT-1706](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1706.md) | Close relationships as including other in the self | Aron, Aron, Tudor & Nelson (1991). In a close relationship the other's resources, perspectives and characteristics are treated as partly one's own: allocations to close others resemble allocations to self, and self/spouse traits are confused in reaction times. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. OpenAlex lists no open copy and an exact-title web search found none posted by an author or publisher; nothing on the Aron lab's pages; perception.org has only a catalogue entry. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Branand, Mashek and Aron 2019 (LIT-1699). |
| [LIT-1711](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1711.md) | The Minimal Group Paradigm and its maximal impact in research on social categorization | A short review of the minimal group paradigm (MGP) after 45 years. Its defining features are a novel, arbitrary and anonymous categorization in which no personal self-interest is served by the allocations. Tajfel's first studies found that fairness guided allocations strongly, but in-group favouritism appeared reliably, and maximizing the in-group's lead over the out-group sometimes beat maximizing its gain. The effect replicated with revised matrices. Critics say it may come from reciprocity expectations or from projecting a positive self onto the new group. It is largely confined to positive resources. When participants can also pay themselves, they take the most for themselves and still favour the in-group with what is left. The paradigm is now used mostly to study other effects of mere categorization: implicit attitudes, face processing, trust, communication. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1301](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1301.md)), in place of [LIT-1697](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1697.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the record's only account, at second hand, of what Tajfel et al. 1971 ([LIT-1697](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1697.md), Unavailable) designed and found, and as a map of the critiques. Two of them bear on the owner's thesis: favouritism may come from projecting the personal self onto the group, and personal gain comes first when it is on offer. |
| [LIT-1714](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1714.md) | The Broken Connection: On Death and the Continuity of Life | Lifton (1979). A psychiatric account of "symbolic immortality": a sense of continuity with what came before and what will come after, sought in five modes, biological (living on through one's children and people), creative (one's works and influence), theological, natural, and experiential transcendence. Its loss underlies much of the psychopathology of death. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher. The Internet Archive holds it only as a lending item; Lifton's own 1973 restatement is closed. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Sturesteps 1992 ([LIT-1689](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1689.md)). |
| [LIT-1721](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1721.md) | Being one of us: we-identities and self-categorization theory | León (2023). A we-identity is one a subject has as a group member, is at times aware of, endorses, and cares about. Self-categorization theory explains we-identities by depersonalization, and phenomenologists (Zahavi, Salice) have adopted it as an account of the "we" in general. But the we-identities of close relationships arise by mutual individualization: partners grasp each other as non-substitutable and complementary. León proposes a socially extended account, drawing on Husserl and integrationist extended-mind criteria. | Active — read in full 2026-10-28 ([NOTE-1309](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1309.md)) from the open-access published article; worth reading as a philosopher's limit on self-categorization theory: the we-identities of close relationships (long friendships, romantic partnerships) rest on mutual individualization and non-substitutability, the opposite of depersonalization, so the theory cannot be the general account of the "we" that phenomenologists have taken it to be. It proposes a socially extended account of such identities. An argument from cases and from relationship research, with no data of its own. Source of [THEORY-1115](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1115.md). |
| [LIT-1723](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1723.md) | Rediscovering the Social Group: A Self-Categorization Theory | Turner, Hogg, Oakes, Reicher and Wetherell (1987), Blackwell. The founding statement of self-categorization theory: personal and social identity are levels of self-categorization, a category becomes salient by meta-contrast and fit, and group behaviour follows from depersonalization, self-perception as an interchangeable exemplar of the ingroup prototype, rather than from attraction or interdependence among members. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-28; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. The Internet Archive holds the 1987 Blackwell printing (rediscoveringsoc0000turn, 266 images) only as a controlled-lending item (access-restricted), which this client cannot borrow. The book has no DOI and no open edition was found. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied: a lawful copy exists, as a lending item ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Turner et al. 1994 (LIT-1794), Skorich's critique (LIT-1765), which quotes chapter 3 with page numbers, León (LIT-1721), Hornsey 2008 (LIT-1742) and Reimer et al. (LIT-1790). |
| [LIT-1726](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1726.md) | Perceiving people as group members: The role of fit in the salience of social categorizations | Oakes, Turner & Haslam (1991). Subjects watching a staged discussion among arts and science students saw the arts/science categorization as most salient when the students disagreed along category lines and in the stereotype-consistent direction: comparative and normative fit together. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. OpenAlex lists no open copy and an exact-title web search found none posted by an author or publisher; UQ eSpace's API refused the request (HTTP 403) and ANU Open Research had no match. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Spears 2021 (LIT-1771). |
| [LIT-1728](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1728.md) v2 | Reinterpreting the empathy–altruism relationship: When one into one equals oneness | Cialdini, Brown, Lewis, Luce & Neuberg (1997). In three questionnaire studies (five tests, N = 90, 74 and 263) students imagined a near stranger, an acquaintance, a friend or a close family member in need and chose how much to help. Closeness raised both empathic concern and "oneness" (the IOS scale with a "we" item). Empathic concern predicted helping, and still did with personal distress and sadness controlled, but with oneness entered it no longer did, while oneness still predicted helping. The authors read empathic concern as a signal of oneness and the helping as "nonaltruistic": with self and other merged, the selfish–selfless distinction "loses its meaning". | Active — read in full 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1444](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1444.md)) from a scan of the published article on a University of Wisconsin course page (https://users.ssc.wisc.edu/~jpiliavi/965/Cialdini%201997.pdf, JPSP 73(3), pp. 481–494, with an OCR text layer); worth reading as the empirical case that helping among close others tracks perceived self–other oneness, not empathic concern. Read it knowing that every helping measure is a hypothetical choice about an imagined person (eviction, orphaned children, a phone call), that the evidence is regression and path analysis of ratings taken after the helping choice, and that the authors call oneness-based helping "nonaltruistic", not egoistic. |
| [LIT-1729](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1729.md) | Empirical Approaches to Altruism | The SEP survey of the empirical egoism–altruism debate, revised in 2025. On the standard account, altruism needs an ultimate desire for another's well-being; biological and social-science senses of "altruism" settle nothing about it. Batson's experiments make a strong case against the aversive-arousal and social-punishment versions of egoism. Self-other merging is a different challenge: only numerical identity with the helped person would make helping egoistic, and none of the four measures used by Cialdini et al. and Batson et al. (IOS, "we", perceived similarity, trait-rating difference) tests for it. The authors report that Batson et al. (1997) avoided Cialdini's methodological problems and found empathy's role "clearly evident", and that a preregistered study (N = 680) supports the empathy–helping link. Altruism is still not shown: divine punishment, principlism, non-moral norms, and habitual or Pavlovian helping remain to be ruled out. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1274](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1274.md)), in place of [LIT-1700](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1700.md) and [LIT-1728](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1728.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the shortest neutral account of the 1997 merging exchange the record holds: it quotes both papers' measures, and it argues that a merging criterion must be one of numerical identity to matter for egoism. It does not report the 1997 results in numbers. |
| [LIT-1735](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1735.md) | Identity fusion: The interplay of personal and social identities in extreme group behavior | Swann, Gómez, Seyle, Morales & Huici (2009). A single pictorial item picks out people "fused" with their country (about 40% of Spanish students): fusion is bimodal, distinct from identification and specific to one group. The fused said they would fight and die for Spain more than other members would, and challenging or activating their personal self raised that further, with no effect on the nonfused. Personal and social identity act together, against self-categorization theory's functional antagonism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1256](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1256.md)) from the published version on the site of co-author Gómez's IDENFUSION group at UNED; worth reading as the record's closest empirical work to the owner's thesis ([CLAIM-491](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-491.md)): a measured self–group overlap in which the personal self is kept, not depersonalized, and in which a challenge to the personal self raises willingness to fight and die for the group. Self-reported intentions, Spanish students only. |
| [LIT-1757](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1757.md) | Who is this "We"? Levels of collective identity and self representations | Brewer & Gardner (1996). Distinguishes three levels of self-representation, personal, relational (interpersonal) and collective (group), each with its own basis of self-worth and frame of reference, and shows that priming "we" shifts self-descriptions and social comparison. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. OpenAlex lists no open copy and an exact-title web search found none posted by an author or publisher; nothing on Ohio State or Northwestern pages; only a Scribd copy, not used. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Brewer 2007 (LIT-1775). |
| [LIT-1759](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1759.md) | Surviving Death | Johnston (2010). Argues that personal identity is response-dependent ("Protean"), so the self-interest that seems to require survival is not fixed; the good person, who identifies with the interests of humanity at large, survives death in the onward life of others. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. The Internet Archive's copy (survivingdeath0000john) is for print-disabled readers only and is not lent, and no open edition was found. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Johnston 2023 ([LIT-1788](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1788.md)), in which Johnston withdraws the book's account of survival. |
| [LIT-1772](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1772.md) | Social identity theory | A textbook chapter. Social identity is "that part of an individual's self-concept which derives from knowledge of membership in a social group (or groups) together with the value or emotional significance attached to that membership" (Tajfel 1978). The theory has two parts. In the first, categorization is always self-relevant, and the motive for a positive social identity drives comparison with out-groups. That identity serves needs for certainty, self-esteem and meaning. In the second, members of low-status groups choose individual mobility, collective action or social creativity, depending on the permeability of group boundaries and the legitimacy and stability of status differences. Identification has cognitive, affective and behavioural components. Applications: identification improves health behaviour and buffers stress; at work it matters more than instrumental interdependence and motivates volunteers. An imagined common in-group raised Italian children's willingness to help an immigrant classmate. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1315](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1315.md)), in place of [LIT-1695](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1695.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as a current statement of social identity theory by two of its principal researchers, read in place of Tajfel & Turner 1979 ([LIT-1695](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1695.md), Unavailable). It is the record's clearest source that the theory builds caring into the definition of social identity while measuring it as a separate component. Uncritical, with no effect sizes. |
| [LIT-1775](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1775.md) | Social Identity and Close Relationships: What is the Connection? | Brewer argues that close relationships and group memberships are two distinct forms of social identity, each a way the individual self is extended to include others: the relational self is personalized (particular, non-interchangeable others), the collective self depersonalized (a symbolic group). They are not two routes to one need for belonging. Measures of group and interpersonal attachment (r = .46 and .33) and of loneliness separate them, and men and women weight them differently. She models each level as a regulatory system balancing opposed needs (uniqueness and similarity; autonomy and intimacy; separation and inclusion), with transfer between them. The model predicts two collectivisms: relational collectivists draw tight in-group boundaries, while individualists identify more readily with large inclusive groups. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1290](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1290.md)), in place of [LIT-1757](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1757.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the tripartite self's author restating it in her own words, with the claim that both relationships and groups extend the self, in two different ways. |
| [LIT-1783](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1783.md) | Empathy, Altruism, and Group Identification | A conceptual paper. It takes Cialdini et al.'s claim that empathy-induced helping is due to self-other merging and asks what "merging" could coherently mean. May argued that every reading either attributes absurd beliefs or fails to explain helping. The authors answer that merging is group identification: in empathizing with Y, X comes to conceive of Y as part of X's social self, so Y's welfare becomes constitutive of "our" welfare. They argue that this reading is behaviourally adequate, because it explains Batson's results in the same way as minimal-group favouritism, and psychologically plausible, because it posits a non-doxastic self-representation rather than a belief in being two bodies. Helping so motivated is then altruistic at the individual level and egoistic at the group level. The empirical dispute with Batson et al. (1997) is set aside. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1277](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1277.md)), in place of [LIT-1728](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1728.md) and [LIT-1700](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1700.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the only work in the record that states the owner's thesis for empathic helping in a precise form: concern for another's welfare is non-instrumental, and that welfare is constitutive of the helper's first-person plural welfare. It offers no measure of group identification apart from empathy. |
| [LIT-1786](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1786.md) | Group-level self-definition and self-investment: A hierarchical (multicomponent) model of in-group identification | In-group identification has five components on two correlated dimensions. Group-level self-definition is individual self-stereotyping (seeing oneself as like the average member) and in-group homogeneity; group-level self-investment is solidarity, satisfaction and centrality. In confirmatory factor analyses of Dutch, European and university identification in two cohorts (N = 464, 363), this model fit better than one-factor, two-factor and cognitive-versus-affective alternatives; the two dimensions correlated .61 to .77. Prospectively, the components predicted different things: centrality predicted perceived threat, homogeneity perceived intergroup difference, and, facing evidence of their group's misdeeds, self-stereotyping predicted group-based guilt while satisfaction and centrality predicted legitimizing the misdeeds. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1262](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1262.md)), in place of [LIT-1795](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1795.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the direct test of whether identification splits into a self-definition and a caring dimension: it does, and they can work against each other. |
| [LIT-1788](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1788.md) | Surviving Death, Again | Johnston (2023). Records "a change in view" from Surviving Death (2010). There he argued that the Christian hope of resurrection fails and offered a this-worldly surrogate, "living on in the onward rush of humankind", built on the idea that we are higher-order things whose deepest future-directed attitudes fix which future embodiments are ours. Now, because reductionist accounts of personal identity breed "fellow travelers" (personites and the like) with moral status and conflicting interests, he holds that we are essentially embodied wills whose present bodies are not essential, so re-embodiment after death is possible. Defines subserving, implementing and interdependence as non-reductive relations between mental and neural events. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1257](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1257.md)) from the published version, open under CC BY-NC-ND at TheoLogica; worth reading as Johnston's own retraction of the account of survival in Surviving Death ([LIT-1759](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1759.md), Unavailable), read in its place. It now holds that we are essentially embodied wills, which drops the self-making view on which the earlier "onward rush of humankind" rested. The paper's own subject is the metaphysics of survival, not altruism. |
| [LIT-1794](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1794.md) | Self and Collective: Cognition and Social Context | Turner, Oakes, Haslam and McGarty (1994). Self-categorization theory's account of self and collective: personal and social identity are different levels of self-categorization, the emergent properties of group processes come from a shift in self-perception from the one to the other, and self-categories are inherently variable and context dependent because they are social comparative and relative to a frame of reference. | Active — read in full 2026-10-28 ([NOTE-1284](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1284.md)) from a scan of the published article supplied by the owner; worth reading as the shortest statement, by its authors, of self-categorization theory's view of the self: personal and social identity are equally authentic levels of self-categorization, salience is readiness times fit (metacontrast and normative fit), and the level, kind, content and prototype of self-categories vary with the comparative frame. It goes on to speculate that the self is generated in context rather than stored. A theoretical paper whose evidence is the group's own studies, reported without data. Source of [THEORY-1114](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1114.md). |
| [LIT-1871](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1871.md) | Why are dreams interesting for philosophers? The example of minimal phenomenal selfhood, plus an agenda for future research | Metzinger (2013), Frontiers in Psychology 4:746. Minimal phenomenal selfhood (MPS), defined by Blanke and Metzinger (2009) as global identification with the body, self-location and a weak first-person perspective, may reduce to transparent spatiotemporal self-location: reports of bodiless dreams and asomatic out-of-body experiences describe a stable self located at an extensionless point, with no body. The paper proposes a phenomenal "unit of identification", an "epistemic agent model" for the knowing self, and a research agenda for dream science, including the test case of phenomenally opaque self-location. No new data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1434](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1434.md)), from the publisher's open-access PDF (frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00746/pdf; also PMC3813926), text extracted with pdftotext. Worth reading as Metzinger's own later statement of minimal phenomenal selfhood: he proposes reducing it to "transparent self-location in a spatiotemporal frame of reference", on the evidence of bodiless dreams and asomatic out-of-body reports, and names, as an open research question, whether any case of phenomenally opaque self-location exists. It is a metatheoretical agenda: it reports survey figures from others and offers no new data, and the decisive case it asks for is not reported. |
| [LIT-1941](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1941.md) | M-Autonomy | Metzinger (2015). M-autonomy is the capacity for second-order mental action, whose central element is veto: rules imposed on one's own mental behaviour, goal selection and permanence, rational guidance, and the intentional inhibition, suspension or ending of an ongoing process. It comes in three degrees: represented knowledge that one has the ability, executed attentional control, and cognitive control. During mind-wandering the ability is kept and its representation in the self-model, the "epistemic agent model", is lost, and an ability is exercised only when so represented. The return of control is represented as self-caused even when an unconscious event caused it, a "functionally adequate form of self-deception". The quantitative argument and the two-thirds figure repeat the 2013 paper's. | Active — read in full 2026-11-01 ([NOTE-1497](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1497.md)), from the author's copy on his Mainz university pages (blogs.uni-mainz.de/fb05philosophie/files/2013/04/Metzinger_M-Autonomy_JCS_2015.pdf, linked from thomasmetzinger.com), typeset with the journal's running heads and pagination, text extracted with pdftotext. Worth reading for the sharpest statement of the will-organization question in Metzinger: what mind-wandering loses is "not the ability itself" but the conscious knowledge of it, and "one can only deliberately and autonomously exert an ability if that ability is explicitly represented in one's phenomenal self-model" ([THEORY-1300](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1300.md)). It also argues that the return of control is represented as self-caused even when an unconscious event caused it ([THEORY-1298](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1298.md)). A development of [LIT-1942](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1942.md) with the empirical detail cut; no new data. |
| [LIT-1942](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1942.md) | The myth of cognitive agency: subpersonal thinking as a cyclically recurring loss of mental autonomy | Metzinger (2013). Mind-wandering is a recurring, unnoticed loss of M-autonomy, the ability to control one's own mental processes, whose defining component is veto: that every ongoing process could be suspended or ended, and that the person knows it. Conscious thought is for the most part subpersonal mental behaviour; it becomes personal-level only when integrated into an "epistemic agent model" (EAM), a transparent self-model of oneself as a knowing, attention-controlling self, which collapses at the onset of each episode. Proposes the "self-representational blink" and a shift in the "unit of identification" to individuate episodes. Its claim that we lack M-autonomy for "roughly two thirds" of conscious life is not borne out by its own minutes, which give about half. | Active — read in full 2026-11-01 ([NOTE-1495](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1495.md)), from the publisher's open-access PDF (frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00931/pdf; also PMC3868016), text extracted with pdftotext. Worth reading as the origin of M-autonomy: the ability to control one's own mental processes, defined by its veto component, and lost without notice in every episode of mind-wandering. It argues that most conscious thought is subpersonal and that a thought becomes the person's only by integration into an "epistemic agent model". The "two thirds of conscious lifetime" without M-autonomy is not what its own figures give: they give about half ([THEORY-1297](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1297.md)). Conceptual work on others' data; no new data. |
| [LIT-1943](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1943.md) | The Elephant and the Blind: The Experience of Pure Consciousness: Philosophy, Science, and 500+ Experiential Reports | Metzinger (2024), MIT Press, open access. More than 500 anonymised reports of "pure awareness" from an online survey of meditators (1,403 usable respondents from 57 countries, 92 questionnaire items, twelve factors), grouped by theme in 34 chapters with commentary. The book's thesis is that consciousness can occur without time, self-location, an egoic self-model or a first-person perspective. It models pure awareness as a highest-level but "nonegoic self-model" of the organism's own epistemic openness, its tonic alertness, and so treats a first-person perspective as content, not a condition, of consciousness. The evidence is retrospective report from a self-selected sample. The methods chapter concedes that such reports cannot show the state was selfless when it occurred, while the summary calls nonegoic consciousness "empirically established". | Active — skimmed 2026-11-01 ([NOTE-1499](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1499.md)), from the publisher's open-access PDF: the introduction, the theoretical commentary of chapters 2, 4, 8, 25, 28 and 31, all of chapter 34 and the epilogue's ethics sections were read; the report chapters were sampled, not read through. Worth reading as the fullest statement of Metzinger's later account of consciousness without a self. It offers "pure awareness" as minimal phenomenal experience and models it as a highest-level but nonegoic model of the organism's own epistemic openness. Its evidence is retrospective, self-selected reports from meditators. The methods chapter concedes the limits of that evidence and the summary overstates what it shows. |
| [LIT-1944](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1944.md) | The Ego Tunnel: The Science of the Mind and the Myth of the Self | Metzinger (2009), Basic Books. The popular statement of the self-model theory of subjectivity: the conscious self is the content of a transparent self-model, and the experienced world is a "tunnel" the brain generates. Unread: registered from its bibliographic records. The theory is read in the record in [LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md) and [LIT-568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-568.md). | Unavailable — registered 2026-11-01 at the owner's request, not read. No lawful open full text was reached, and the book is in copyright with Basic Books. OpenAlex has no record of the book. Google Books shows no viewable edition. The Internet Archive's copy (egotunnelscience0000metz) is in its print-disabled and lending collections, which require a borrowing account, so it is not an open copy. No author-posted copy was found. The theory it popularises is read in the record in [LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md) and [LIT-568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-568.md), and its later development in [LIT-1943](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1943.md). It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-1945](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1945.md) | The Problem of Mental Action: Predictive Control without Sensory Sheets | Metzinger (2017), in Philosophy and Predictive Processing. Mental action cannot be active inference through the body, since no sensory sheet is in the loop; it is offered instead as predictive control of effective connectivity aimed at the epistemic value of states in the self-model. Attentional agency controls precision expectations of an internal model. Cognitive agency selects among candidate thoughts that mind-wandering continually generates ("mental sleep-walking"), and M-autonomy lets the system "actively sculpt its own internal affordance landscape". Whether the conscious epistemic agent model constitutes this control, represents and enables it, or is a phenomenal artefact, current data "do not help to decide". Agency's sense of origination may be an enculturated post-hoc confabulation. | Active — read in full 2026-11-01 ([NOTE-1496](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1496.md)), from the open-access PDF on the collection's own site (predictive-mind.net/papers/the-problem-of-mental-action/at_download/paperPDF), text extracted with pdftotext. Worth reading for two things the 2013 and 2015 papers lack: a model of mental action as selection from a competition among candidate thoughts that mind-wandering supplies (the "cognitive affordance hypothesis"), and a plain statement that the data cannot yet decide whether the epistemic agent model constitutes mental control, represents and enables it, or is a phenomenal by-product ([THEORY-1296](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1296.md)). That withholds what M-autonomy ([LIT-1941](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1941.md)) asserted as a principle. Four testable hypotheses, none tested; no data. |
| [LIT-1946](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1946.md) | Minimal phenomenal experience: Meditation, tonic alertness, and the phenomenology of “pure” consciousness | Metzinger (2020), Philosophy and the Mind Sciences 1(I):7. Proposes minimal phenomenal experience (MPE) as a candidate for the simplest consciousness and the entry point to a "minimal model" explanation. MPE is to lack minimal phenomenal selfhood, time and a spatial frame. Six constraints are drawn from contemplative and Western texts: Wakefulness, Low Complexity, Self-Luminosity, Introspective Availability, Epistemicity and Transparency/Opacity. Sixteen case studies flesh them out. The hypothesis: pure awareness is a temporally thin Bayesian representation of the organism's tonic alertness, a model of an "unpartitioned epistemic space". It "definitely has representational content" and is "non-egoic self-modelling". Tonic alertness without that model, as in unresponsive wakefulness, is not conscious. A conceptual paper. Its evidence is quoted report. | Active — read in full 2026-11-01 ([NOTE-1498](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1498.md)) from the journal's open-access PDF. Worth reading as the founding statement of minimal phenomenal experience, the concept the record's reading of Chandia-Jorquera et al. ([LIT-1354](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1354.md)) takes as given. It holds that pure awareness has representational content: a temporally thin, nonegoic model of the organism's tonic alertness, its "epistemic space". On that account, consciousness without a self-model in the egoic sense still involves self-modelling, and it lacks even a phenomenal quality of oneness. Its evidence is sixteen quoted reports and texts. Its methodological problems, performative self-contradiction among them, are deferred to other papers. |
